1.1 Quality and pertinence of the project's research and innovation objectives (and the extent to which they are ambitious, and go beyond the state of the art)

**The research problem and its pertinence**

Irrigation decisions for row crops must be made under compounding uncertainty. The true agronomic state of the field — root-zone soil moisture, crop water status, canopy development, biomass — is only partially observable at the moment of decision, and the outcome of each irrigation choice depends on weather that has not yet materialised. Prior work in this domain has overwhelmingly responded to this challenge by producing point estimates: a single best-guess soil moisture value, a deterministic crop-water-stress index, a rule-based irrigation trigger. What is missing, as the systematic literature review underpinning this project establishes, is a framework that instead carries uncertainty honestly from multi-sensor observation through probabilistic field-state diagnosis all the way into an uncertainty-aware irrigation decision recommendation — a framework in which every output reports not only what the state is but how confident the model is, and in which that confidence propagates without collapsing into the final agronomic advice.

This project resolves that structural gap by constructing an end-to-end uncertainty chain for tomato (research decision RQ1), applying it at Hungarian tomato field sites accessed through the associated partner AgroVIR, and validating it against non-destructive physiological ground truth collected by a researcher whose doctoral expertise is precisely that measurement domain. The project is submitted as a 24-month European Postdoctoral Fellowship by Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, under the supervision of Dr. András Jung. The research is pertinent to the MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships 2026 call (HORIZON-MSCA-2026-PF-01) because it unites an excellent, internationally mobile researcher with a host whose competences are genuinely complementary to hers, in pursuit of a scientific objective whose novelty is narrow, defensible, and grounded in a documented literature gap.

**Architecture of the five objectives**

The project defines five objectives. The first four (OBJ-1 through OBJ-4) are scientific and technical; the fifth (OBJ-5) is the MSCA-PF developmental objective mandated by the instrument. Together they form a coherent scientific architecture in which the diagnostic branch (OBJ-1) produces a calibrated posterior over the latent field state, the prognostic branch (OBJ-2) turns that posterior into an uncertainty-aware irrigation recommendation optimised for water-use efficiency, the validation protocol (OBJ-3) establishes whether both branches are credible, and the research demonstrator (OBJ-4) integrates the full pipeline into a working end-to-end artefact. The career-development objective (OBJ-5) structures the transfer of knowledge and competences that gives the fellowship its MSCA rationale. Each objective is examined in turn below.

---

**OBJ-1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the latent field state**

The first objective is to develop and calibrate a probabilistic diagnostic method that fuses multi-source Earth-observation and field-observation data into posterior estimates of the latent field state of a tomato crop. The confirmed target field state (research decision RQ3) comprises root-zone soil moisture and crop water status. The data streams entering the diagnostic model are Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical imagery, and secured high-resolution PlanetScope data (access confirmed via the Planet platform and API, research decision RQ8), supplemented by ERA5 meteorological reanalysis and field observations.

The project adopts Route B — the homogeneous-patch proxy — as its primary diagnostic route (research decision RQ2). Route B sidesteps the sub-pixel resolution problem that afflicts coarse-pixel satellite data when applied to heterogeneous agricultural landscapes. Rather than attempting to disaggregate a coarse pixel into sub-pixel contributions from different land cover types, Route B identifies a nearby homogeneous patch — matched on high-resolution soil and climate covariates — whose biology covaries with the target tomato crop and which the coarse satellite pixel can read cleanly without any disaggregation step. The EO data thereby resolve the proxy patch at native resolution; the proxy patch reading is then used to infer the target crop's field state, on the strength of the demonstrated covariation between patch and crop.

The methodological architecture simultaneously defines Route A — direct probabilistic fusion — as a rigorous alternative within the same framework. In Route A, the satellite observations enter a probabilistic machine-learning model (candidate families: Bayesian hierarchical model, Gaussian process, probabilistic machine learning more broadly) as one more covariate alongside radar, optical, meteorological, soil and field-observation data, going directly to the posterior over the field state in a single modelling step. This one-step approach avoids any intermediate pixel-level representation and the associated error amplification, but is more demanding in terms of training data and model complexity. Both routes produce the same output currency — a posterior distribution over root-zone soil moisture and crop water status — and both routes feed the same downstream decision engine (OBJ-2).

The measurable target for OBJ-1 is a calibrated diagnostic model that outputs root-zone soil moisture and crop water status with explicit, honest uncertainty expressed as posterior or prediction intervals. The verifiable criterion is not a fabricated accuracy percentage but the calibration quality of the reported intervals, assessed through the validation protocol of OBJ-3: specifically, whether 90% prediction intervals contain the truth approximately 90% of the time (research decision RQ5). This criterion is specific, computable from any validation dataset using standard frequentist coverage methods, and reproducible by any independent third party.

OBJ-1 is delivered through WP1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state, with the primary deliverable D1-01: Multi-sensor data harmonisation and diagnostic model report (due month 14).

---

**OBJ-2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine for water-use-efficient irrigation choice**

The second objective is to develop the prognostic decision engine that converts the diagnosed field state into an irrigation recommendation, propagating the uncertainty from OBJ-1 through to the final advice without collapsing it. The engine operates in three coupled stages.

In the first stage, the FAO AquaCrop crop model is calibrated in an uncertainty-aware way: rather than identifying a single best-fit parameter set, the calibration retains an honest posterior distribution over the model's parameters, keeping the model's parametric uncertainty explicit. This approach, building on established uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration methods in the literature, ensures that the model's predictions reflect both its structural limitations and the information content of the available observations. The uncertainty-aware calibration is the project's vault-grounded methodology; it is not a novel claim of the fellow but a deliberate design choice grounded in prior work.

In the second stage, the calibrated AquaCrop instance runs counterfactual irrigation simulations over weather ensembles. For each candidate irrigation decision, the engine evaluates crop yield and water use not under a single deterministic weather trajectory but over the distribution of plausible future weather realisations (drawn from ERA5 climatology or similar ensemble sources). This produces, for each candidate decision, a distribution of agricultural outcomes rather than a single point forecast.

In the third stage, the candidate decisions are ranked by their expected water-use efficiency (WUE, research decision RQ6), and the option with the best expected WUE under joint weather and model uncertainty is recommended. Water-use efficiency is the confirmed decision objective for the validation phase. The decision-engine architecture is kept open to alternative objective formulations — including profit-based or drought-risk-based scoring — but WUE is the verified criterion for OBJ-3's validation.

The measurable target for OBJ-2 is an integrated decision engine that scores candidate irrigation decisions by WUE under joint model and weather uncertainty, with uncertainty propagated from OBJ-1's diagnosis into the recommendation, and that produces recommendations on Hungarian tomato farms at the spatial and temporal resolution supported by the available Earth-observation data. The pilot success criterion is that the full pipeline — from diagnosis to recommendation — meets OBJ-3's uncertainty-calibration test (research decision RQ7).

OBJ-2 is delivered through WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration, with the primary deliverable D2-01: Decision engine and research demonstrator report (due month 20).

---

**OBJ-3: Field validation and honest uncertainty calibration**

The third objective is to design and execute a validation protocol that establishes, on real tomato farms under real growing-season conditions, whether the diagnostic model (OBJ-1) and the decision recommendations (OBJ-2) are credible and whether the reported uncertainty is well calibrated. The validation protocol rests on four confirmed elements, each a concrete and independently evaluable criterion.

First, ground truth (research decision RQ4): the validation collects non-destructive physiological measurements — chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance — at the field sites. These measurements are the fellow's confirmed domain expertise, established through a summa cum laude doctoral thesis on the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants. The choice of non-destructive methods reflects both methodological rigour (these measurements do not disturb the plant, allowing repeated measurement at the same plants over the season) and the direct load-bearing link between the fellow's prior training and the project's ground-truth protocol.

Second, the uncertainty-calibration criterion (research decision RQ5): 90% prediction intervals produced by the diagnostic model must contain the ground-truth measurement approximately 90% of the time. This is a frequency-coverage criterion: it tests not whether the model is accurate in expectation but whether its reported confidence is honest. A model that always produces extremely wide intervals trivially satisfies this criterion; the conjunction with OBJ-2's WUE optimisation requires intervals to be informative enough to discriminate between candidate irrigation decisions. The combination of coverage (RQ5) and usefulness (OBJ-2's WUE recommendation improving over a baseline) constitutes the full verification standard.

Third, the pilot success criterion (research decision RQ7): the project is considered scientifically successful if the RQ5 calibration target is met on the validation set. This is a binary pass/fail criterion applied to the primary research deliverable; it is not a subjective assessment.

Fourth, Route B patch-covariation proof (research decision RQ9): Route B's scientific premise — that the homogeneous proxy patch covaries sufficiently with the target tomato crop to serve as a faithful proxy — must be demonstrated empirically rather than assumed. The project tests this via a co-located seasonal measurement campaign in which the target tomato crop and the proxy patch are measured simultaneously at the same field sites over at least one full growing season, establishing statistical covariation between the proxy readings and the reference plant-physiology measurements. An experimental extension of Route B — the control-stand variant — deliberately plants a covarying species as a designed proxy sensor, making the covariation measurable by design rather than reliant on naturally occurring patch selection. If the co-located campaign does not establish sufficient statistical covariation, this is reported as a negative result: the Route B premise fails for the chosen patch configuration, Route A becomes the primary pathway, and the negative result is itself a publishable and scientifically valuable contribution to the literature on proxy-based field-state estimation.

A coherence caveat is recorded transparently: the RQ4 non-destructive physiological measures validate the crop-water-status component of the target field state (RQ3) directly, but validate the root-zone soil moisture component only indirectly (as plant-physiology stress responses reflect, with some lag and integration, the soil water available to the root zone). No soil-moisture sensor plan beyond the confirmed ground-truth protocol is fabricated; this design constraint is acknowledged and to be addressed in the detailed validation protocol as part of WP3.

Field sites are Hungarian tomato farms accessed through AgroVIR, which provides farmer access, field logistics, and grower feedback throughout the growing seasons.

OBJ-3 is delivered through WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration, with the primary deliverable D3-01: Field validation and uncertainty calibration report (due month 24).

---

**OBJ-4: Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP)**

The fourth objective is to integrate the diagnostic model (OBJ-1) and the decision engine (OBJ-2) into a standalone research demonstrator — a web minimum viable product — that presents irrigation recommendations together with their uncertainty in a form legible to potential end users. The demonstrator exercises the full observation-to-decision pipeline: data ingestion, probabilistic diagnosis, uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration and counterfactual simulation, WUE-optimised recommendation, and uncertainty visualisation.

The demonstrator is explicitly positioned as a research artefact rather than an operational product. The TRL target is a research prototype, TRL 3–4 (research decision RQ10), which is the level appropriate to a 24-month European Postdoctoral Fellowship. TRL 3 corresponds to experimental proof of concept; TRL 4 corresponds to technology validated in a laboratory or controlled environment. The project does not claim to deliver an operational irrigation management system ready for commercial deployment; it claims to deliver a working research prototype that demonstrates the end-to-end feasibility of the uncertainty chain and provides an open-software artefact that the community can build on. AgroVIR assists with the demonstrator through farmer access and grower feedback; it does not own or operate the tool.

The measurable target for OBJ-4 is a working end-to-end demonstrator that can ingest multi-source EO data, execute the full pipeline, and return an irrigation recommendation with its uncertainty to the user interface. The deliverable is principally D2-01: Decision engine and research demonstrator report (due month 20).

---

**OBJ-5: Advancement of the fellow's competences and career**

The fifth objective is the MSCA-PF instrument's developmental objective: to advance Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's scientific, technical and transferable competences and career perspectives through the fellowship's training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge. By month 24 of the fellowship, the measurable and verifiable outputs of OBJ-5 are: a Career Development Plan prepared jointly by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and submitted as a project deliverable at the start of the action (deliverable D4-01: Career Development Plan, due month 3), then reviewed and updated during the fellowship; structured transferable-skills training integrating all MSCA-PF mandatory training dimensions — digital and AI skills including the responsible use of generative AI in remote-sensing, crop-water modelling and scientific coding; knowledge valorisation; innovation and entrepreneurship; research integrity; and open science and FAIR data stewardship; peer-reviewed publication and conference dissemination of the project's results; and two-way transfer of knowledge between the fellow and the host group, evidenced by substantive methods exchange in both directions. Specific quantitative targets for publications, training hours, thesis co-supervision, and similar metrics are not pre-asserted here; consistent with the project's commitment to measurability over assertion, these targets are to be fixed jointly in the Career Development Plan with the supervisor, ensuring they are grounded in the real supervision context rather than generic ambitions.

The two-way transfer is bidirectional and substantive. Dr. Rositsa Cholakova brings plant-physiology and non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise — the project's biological ground-truth engine (RQ4) — into ELTE's Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics. Dr. András Jung and the host group provide remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy, and multisensor-drone fusion methods and infrastructure in return. This is a genuine exchange that neither party could replicate unilaterally: the fellow's domain secures the validity of the validation protocol; the host's domain enables the multi-sensor EO fusion that gives the project its diagnostic breadth. The two-way transfer constitutes a real interdisciplinary crossing — from plant physiology to geoinformatics and back — rather than a token training supplement to an otherwise independent research programme.

OBJ-5 is delivered through WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge, with the primary deliverable D4-01: Career Development Plan (due month 3).

---

**Measurability, verifiability and realistic achievability of the objectives**

Four of the five objectives carry explicitly testable success criteria:

OBJ-1 is verifiable through OBJ-3's uncertainty-calibration test: the diagnostic model either meets the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) on the held-out validation dataset or it does not. The criterion is computable from any labelled validation dataset using standard interval-coverage methods and is reproducible by any independent assessor. The deliverable D1-01 documents the model, the calibration record and the assessment against RQ5.

OBJ-2 is verifiable in the same validation exercise: the decision engine either produces recommendations that improve expected WUE under joint model and weather uncertainty relative to a baseline irrigation strategy, or it does not. The pilot success criterion (RQ7) — that the RQ5 calibration target is met on the validation set — is the formal pass/fail threshold. D2-01 documents the engine, its WUE scoring, and the validation performance.

OBJ-3 is self-defining in measurable terms. Four ground-truth measurement types (RQ4) are specified by instrument: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy/leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance. One calibration criterion is stated as a frequency coverage rate (RQ5): 90% intervals must contain the truth approximately 90% of the time. One success criterion is a binary application of RQ5 on the validation set (RQ7). One covariation test is a statistical comparison of simultaneously collected time series from the proxy patch and the target crop (RQ9). All four are third-party reproducible from the documented measurement protocols and data, which are to be released as open data under FAIR principles. D3-01 provides the documented validation dataset, calibration evidence, and covariation test results.

OBJ-4 is verifiable by the existence and functioning of the research demonstrator: the artefact either exercises the full observation-to-decision pipeline and produces a recommendation with uncertainty output, or it does not. The TRL 3–4 assessment criterion is operational correctness at the prototype level, not commercial readiness.

OBJ-5 is partially measurable through the timely delivery and content of D4-01 (Career Development Plan, due month 3), the training activities logged in WP4, and the publication and dissemination record at month 24. The deliberate deferral of specific quantitative targets to the Career Development Plan is not a gap in measurability but a principled design choice: it ensures that the targets are set in the real supervision context by the supervisor and fellow jointly (as required by the MSCA-PF Career Development Plan mandate, scope requirement SR-07), rather than pre-determined without knowledge of the host environment.

The objectives are realistically achievable within 24 months. The data and infrastructure on which the research depends are secured before the fellowship begins: PlanetScope access is confirmed via the Planet platform and API (RQ8); Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 are open Copernicus data requiring no access negotiation; ERA5 reanalysis is freely available from ECMWF; and Hungarian tomato field sites are accessible through the confirmed associated partner AgroVIR. The fellow's ground-truth expertise (non-destructive physiological measurement, RQ4) is her doctoral specialisation and requires no acquisition during the fellowship. The supervisor's expertise in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, and multisensor-drone fusion is directly aligned with the EO data streams the project employs, and is confirmed as available at ELTE's Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics. The primary methodological risk is Route B's patch-covariation assumption: the project addresses this as a first-class scientific question (RQ9) with a built-in contingency (Route A remains defined within the same architectural framework and can serve as the primary pathway if the co-located campaign does not demonstrate sufficient covariation). This risk-managed design — two interchangeable diagnostic routes sharing one decision engine — means that scientific failure of Route B's covariation premise is not a project failure but a research finding.

The sequencing of deliverables confirms the feasibility of the timeline. The diagnostic model report (D1-01) falls at month 14, ensuring that OBJ-1 is concluded before the decision engine report (D2-01) at month 20, which in turn precedes the final validation report (D3-01) at month 24. WP3's field validation campaigns are co-timed with the growing season and begin early in the fellowship so that at least one full seasonal dataset is available for calibration and at least one for held-out validation, consistent with a 24-month timeline for tomato production in Hungary.

---

**Going beyond the state of the art: the research gap and the novelty claim**

The project's novelty claim is argued against a systematic literature review of multi-sensor crop-water-stress monitoring studies. The literature review, anchored in a research-gap matrix constructed across the body of reviewed studies, organises published work by two gradients: sensor-integration depth on one axis and task complexity — ranging from crop-water-stress detection, through yield estimation and irrigation optimisation, to real-time decision support — on the other. As both gradients increase in tandem, the count of published papers falls sharply: the field has been most active in detection with single or dual sensors, and progressively thinner as the sensor suite broadens and the task moves toward decision support. The two gradients meet in the single empty cell of the matrix: real-time decision support integrated with high-resolution PlanetScope imagery. This cell is the gap the project targets.

The PlanetScope dimension of the gap is not incidental. PlanetScope's sub-5-metre spatial resolution is the data source that enables Route B's core operation: identifying a homogeneous proxy patch that a coarse pixel can read cleanly. At Sentinel-2's 10-metre native resolution, heterogeneous agricultural fields generate substantial within-pixel mixing, making it difficult to attribute coarse-pixel spectral signatures to a single crop type or growth state. PlanetScope's higher resolution supports the patch-selection step of Route B without sub-pixel disaggregation, and is the EO stream most naturally paired with the project's proxy-patch architecture. The fact that PlanetScope integration with real-time decision support is the single empty cell in the gap matrix is therefore structurally coherent with the project's methodological choice.

The novelty framing, argued as a synthesis from the literature review, is the following: while multimodal data fusion for crop-water-stress monitoring is a mature research domain — with established single-epoch and time-series methods combining radar, optical and ancillary data — the literature does not contain an end-to-end framework that combines all three of the following simultaneously: (i) learned multimodal fusion of multi-resolution EO data into (ii) explicit probabilistic crop-water-state estimation with calibrated uncertainty, feeding into (iii) economically or agronomically optimised irrigation decision support under that uncertainty. Genuine probabilistic precedents exist and are respected in the review: Bayesian maximum entropy methods have been applied to drought fusion; copula-based approaches have been used to link drought indices to irrigation scheduling; dynamic Bayesian networks have been applied to plant-stress diagnosis; and multi-feature fusion networks have been proposed for crop-stress classification. None of these combines all three elements — learned multimodal EO fusion, explicit calibrated probabilistic crop-water-state output, and optimised irrigation decision under that uncertainty — end-to-end.

The novelty claim is deliberately narrow and carefully bounded. It does not assert novelty in any single component: probabilistic machine learning is a well-established field; AquaCrop is a widely used FAO crop model; Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 fusion for agriculture is established practice; PlanetScope has been used in agronomic studies. The claim is specifically that the end-to-end coupling of these elements — with an honest uncertainty chain from observation to decision — is underdeveloped in the reviewed literature, and that this project addresses that gap in a targeted, measurable, and falsifiable way.

The uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration component builds on established approaches for uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration (documented in the literature, e.g. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2022.105556). The project's contribution is not a new AquaCrop calibration method but the coupling of a calibrated, uncertainty-retaining AquaCrop instance to an upstream probabilistic diagnostic model and a downstream WUE-optimised decision engine, with the uncertainty chain kept intact across all three stages.

---

**Extent to which the work is ambitious**

The project is ambitious along three distinct and complementary dimensions, all of which are consistent with and appropriate to a 24-month European Postdoctoral Fellowship.

Scientific ambition. The commitment to an honest end-to-end uncertainty chain is more demanding than any approach in the reviewed literature. The vast majority of existing crop-water-stress monitoring systems, and virtually all existing irrigation decision-support tools, produce point estimates of soil moisture or crop stress and deterministic irrigation recommendations. This project's methodological commitment is to report every stage as a distribution — a posterior over the field state, an ensemble of future weather realisations, a distribution of WUE outcomes for each candidate decision — and to verify that the distributions are honest, not merely nominally probabilistic. The verification criterion (90% prediction-interval coverage, RQ5) is specifically designed to distinguish honest uncertainty from overconfident or underconfident reporting. This is scientifically more demanding than showing that the model is more accurate than a baseline; it requires that the model knows what it does not know.

Methodological ambition. The control-stand variant of Route B — deliberately planting a covarying species as a designed proxy sensor — extends the proxy-patch concept beyond opportunistic patch selection into a controlled experimental design in which covariation is engineered and measured by construction. This methodological extension is novel within the proxy-vegetation literature, and the project's commitment to prove rather than assume patch covariation (RQ9) represents a methodological standard higher than what prior works in this area have typically adopted. The co-located seasonal campaign required to test covariation is resource-intensive and adds scientific risk, but it also produces definitive evidence on the validity of the proxy approach rather than an unverified assumption that could later undermine the framework's credibility.

Developmental ambition. The fellowship crosses a genuine disciplinary boundary. Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's research profile to date is rooted in plant physiology — non-destructive evaluation of abiotic plant stress and crop monitoring, with doctoral work on drought-stressed tomato plants. ELTE's Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, led by Dr. András Jung, occupies a different disciplinary space: remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, multisensor-drone fusion, and geoinformatics. The two-way transfer of knowledge between these domains — plant-physiology expertise flowing from the fellow into the host's remote-sensing group; EO methodology and infrastructure flowing in the opposite direction — produces a researcher with a competence profile that very few individuals in the field of precision agriculture currently hold: deep experimental knowledge of plant-stress physiology combined with operational proficiency in probabilistic multi-sensor EO fusion. This combination is directly relevant to the growing need for grounded, biologically validated remote-sensing-based agricultural decision support, and it is a profile that cannot be acquired by training within either discipline alone.

The TRL target (research prototype, TRL 3–4, RQ10) is proportionate and honest. The project does not claim to deliver an operational irrigation management system deployable at commercial scale. It claims to deliver a validated, uncertainty-calibrated research prototype that demonstrates the end-to-end feasibility of the uncertainty chain, contributes open research software and open validation data under FAIR principles, and provides the scientific community with a reproducible foundation for subsequent applied-research programmes targeting higher TRL levels. This is the ambition appropriate to a 24-month fellowship: to advance the state of the art at the frontier of feasibility demonstration, not to pre-empt the applied-development pathway that follows from it.

sub_sections.title: Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)

**1.2 Soundness of the proposed methodology (including interdisciplinary approaches, consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects if relevant for the research project, and the quality of open science practices)**

---

**The unifying methodological principle: an honest uncertainty chain from observation to decision**

The project's methodology is organised around a single architectural commitment: to carry uncertainty honestly from the first act of observation all the way through to the final irrigation recommendation, without collapsing it into a point estimate at any intermediate stage. This commitment is the project's core conceptual model and the standard against which every methodological choice is evaluated. It implies that every output of the pipeline — the diagnosed field state, the crop-model parameter posterior, the simulated yield distribution, the ranked candidate irrigation decisions — must be reported as a distribution, not a single value, and that the distributions must be empirically verified to be calibrated. The verifiability criterion is explicit: 90% prediction intervals must contain the truth approximately 90% of the time (RQ5). This is not an accuracy claim. It is a coverage claim — a test of whether the model's reported confidence is honest, not merely whether the model's central estimate is close to the truth.

This framing drives an important distinction from the majority of the reviewed literature, which the field-objectives section has already established is dominated by point-estimate methods. The present methodology is more demanding than point-estimate approaches: it requires that the probabilistic machinery propagate distributions through each stage without discretising them, and that the decision engine acts on those distributions rather than on the point estimates it might more conveniently extract from them. The entire design, from data ingestion through AquaCrop calibration to final decision scoring, is shaped by this requirement.

The methodology decomposes into two sequential scientific blocks — a diagnostic branch (WP1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) and a prognostic branch (WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) — tied together by the uncertainty chain that runs through both. Both blocks are validated in a third block (WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration). The three scientific work packages operate in parallel or overlapping temporal windows: WP1 runs from month 1 through month 14; WP2 from month 6 through month 20; WP3 from month 8 through month 24.

---

**The diagnostic branch: two routes, one decision engine, one shared uncertainty currency**

The diagnostic branch addresses the problem of estimating the latent field state — root-zone soil moisture and crop water status — from multiple uncertain, heterogeneous data sources. The confirmed target field state comprises both these quantities simultaneously (RQ3). The data streams entering the diagnosis are: Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter (open Copernicus data), Sentinel-2 multispectral optical imagery (open Copernicus data), high-resolution PlanetScope imagery (access secured via the Planet platform and API, RQ8), ERA5 meteorological reanalysis from ECMWF, and in-field observations. These streams differ in spatial resolution, temporal cadence, acquisition geometry, wavelength, and noise characteristics. Their harmonisation into a coherent multi-temporal multi-resolution data object, on a geospatial and time-series platform, is the first technical task of WP1 and the subject of milestone MS1 (due month 6), which verifies that Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, soil-sensor and weather data are ingested, quality-controlled and harmonised over the field boundaries on the geospatial/time-series platform.

The diagnostic branch is architecturally designed around two interchangeable routes that share one downstream decision engine and produce outputs in the same currency — a posterior distribution over the target field state — so that either route can feed the prognostic branch without redesign.

**Route B — Homogeneous Patch Proxy** is the confirmed primary diagnostic route (RQ2). Route B sidesteps the sub-pixel resolution problem that afflicts coarse-resolution satellite data when applied to heterogeneous agricultural landscapes. Rather than attempting to decompose a mixed-pixel spectral signature into its constituent land-cover contributions — a sub-pixel disaggregation step that amplifies noise and introduces its own assumptions — Route B identifies a nearby homogeneous patch that is matched to the target tomato crop on high-resolution soil and climate covariates. This patch's biology is assumed to covary with the target crop; because the patch is homogeneous at native EO resolution, the coarse satellite pixel can read it cleanly without any disaggregation. The proxy patch reading is then used to infer the target field state, on the strength of the measured covariation. Route B therefore transforms the sub-pixel problem into a covariation problem: the critical assumption shifts from 'we can decompose this mixed pixel' to 'this patch genuinely covaries with this crop'. The latter assumption is testable by direct measurement, and testing it is a first-class research commitment of the project (RQ9, addressed in WP3).

The methodological architecture simultaneously defines Route A — Direct Probabilistic Fusion — as the rigorous alternative. In Route A, all data streams enter a probabilistic machine-learning model (candidate families: Bayesian hierarchical model, Gaussian process, or probabilistic machine learning more broadly) as simultaneous covariates, and the model maps them directly to the posterior over the latent field state in a single inference step. Route A makes no intermediate pixel-level representation, but is correspondingly more demanding in terms of training data, model complexity, computational infrastructure, and the modelling expertise required to implement and calibrate a high-dimensional probabilistic model. Both routes produce outputs in the same posterior format; both feed the same AquaCrop decision engine; and the methodological commitment to uncertainty calibration (RQ5) applies identically to both.

The two-route design is a deliberate risk-management strategy, not methodological indecision. Route A is kept defined within the same modelling framework so that it can serve as comparison or contingency at any point during WP1. Route B is the primary route because its lower computational and data demands make it more tractable within a 24-month fellowship, and because the homogeneous-patch concept uniquely benefits from the confirmed PlanetScope data (RQ8): PlanetScope's sub-5-metre spatial resolution supports the patch-selection step of Route B without sub-pixel disaggregation, making PlanetScope the natural EO stream for this architecture. If the co-located seasonal campaign in WP3 does not demonstrate sufficient covariation between the proxy patch and the target tomato crop, Route A becomes the primary diagnostic pathway and the negative covariation result is documented as a finding (see the challenge section below).

The critical unverified assumption of Route B — that the chosen homogeneous patch genuinely covaries with the target crop — is treated as a first-class scientific question rather than a background assumption. Route B's experimental extension — the control-stand variant — deliberately plants a covarying species adjacent to the target tomato crop as a designed proxy sensor, making covariation measurable by construction rather than reliant on the opportunistic selection of naturally occurring patches. The co-located seasonal measurement campaign (RQ9) measures both the target tomato crop and the proxy patch simultaneously throughout at least one full growing season at the Hungarian field sites, producing a time series from which statistical covariation can be directly assessed.

---

**The prognostic branch: uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration, counterfactual simulation, and WUE-optimised recommendation**

From the diagnosed field state — whether produced by Route A or Route B — the prognostic branch takes over and translates the state distribution into an irrigation recommendation. This branch has three coupled stages, each of which preserves and propagates the uncertainty carried from the diagnostic branch.

In the first stage, the FAO AquaCrop crop model is calibrated in an uncertainty-aware way. Standard AquaCrop calibration fits a single best-estimate parameter set; this collapses the model's parametric uncertainty and produces overconfident projections. The uncertainty-aware calibration adopted here instead fits a posterior distribution over the model's parameters, retaining an honest parameter range consistent with the available observations. This approach builds on established methods for uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration in the literature (doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2022.105556); the project's contribution is the integration of this calibration approach with an upstream probabilistic diagnostic model and the downstream decision engine, with the uncertainty chain kept intact across all three stages. The risk of collapsing to a single overconfident parameter set (RISK-08) is the principal modelling risk of the prognostic branch, and the uncertainty-aware calibration protocol is the primary mitigation: the verifiable output is that the AquaCrop instance returns a parameter posterior, not a point estimate, and that this posterior propagates into the simulation outputs.

In the second stage, the calibrated AquaCrop instance runs counterfactual irrigation simulations. For each candidate irrigation decision — each distinct decision about whether to irrigate, how much, and when — the engine evaluates the distribution of future crop yields and water use over a weather ensemble drawn from the ERA5 climatological record. This produces, for each candidate decision, a distribution of agronomic outcomes under the joint uncertainty of model parameters and future weather, rather than a single deterministic forecast. The ensemble size is calibrated to be computationally tractable within the fellowship's infrastructure while providing stable distributional estimates; the ERA5-based climatological ensemble is the confirmed meteorological source, with no additional proprietary weather data required.

In the third stage, the candidate decisions are scored by their expected water-use efficiency (WUE, RQ6) computed under the joint parameter-and-weather uncertainty, and the option with the best expected WUE is recommended. WUE is the confirmed decision objective for the validation phase; the prognostic branch's machinery is kept general enough to accommodate alternative objective functions (profit-based, drought-risk-based) but the verification criterion used in OBJ-3's validation protocol is WUE. The scored recommendation is not a single point — it reports the expected WUE and the uncertainty of that expectation — enabling the end user to appreciate not only which decision is recommended but how reliable the recommendation is.

The full pipeline from data ingestion through diagnosis through AquaCrop simulation through WUE-scored recommendation is integrated into a standalone research demonstrator (WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), a web minimum viable product (web MVP) that presents irrigation recommendations together with their uncertainty at a level appropriate to a research prototype, TRL 3–4 (RQ10). The demonstrator does not claim operational readiness for commercial deployment; it demonstrates end-to-end pipeline feasibility and serves as the open research artefact through which the scientific community can access and evaluate the integrated method.

---

**The validation protocol: field-grounded, criterion-explicit, risk-managed**

The validation protocol (WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) is built around four explicit, independently evaluable criteria, each grounded in the project's research decisions. The criteria are stated before the fellowship begins, not post-hoc — this pre-registration of success criteria is itself a methodological commitment to intellectual honesty.

Ground-truth measurements (RQ4) are collected using non-destructive physiological instruments: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance. These four measurement types are the direct domain expertise of Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, established through her doctoral thesis (summa cum laude, 2020) on the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527). The choice of non-destructive methods is not incidental: non-destructive instruments do not disturb the plant, enabling repeated measurement at the same individuals over the growing season and providing the high-temporal-density time series that the calibration and validation protocol requires. The direct load-bearing link between the fellow's prior training and the project's ground-truth protocol is one of the principal merits of this fellow-host pairing: the validation protocol's validity rests on expert measurement practice, not equipment alone.

Field sites are Hungarian tomato farms accessed through the confirmed associated partner AgroVIR. AgroVIR provides farmer access, field logistics, and grower feedback throughout the growing seasons; it does not own or operate the research demonstrator. The co-located seasonal measurement campaign (RQ9) — measuring target crop and proxy patch simultaneously over at least one full growing season — is conducted at these sites.

The uncertainty-calibration criterion (RQ5) assesses whether 90% prediction intervals produced by the diagnostic model contain the ground-truth measurement approximately 90% of the time. This frequentist coverage test requires that the intervals be both honest (not systematically too narrow, which would yield coverage below 90%) and informative (not trivially wide, which would provide no discriminative value for the decision engine). The combination of the coverage criterion (RQ5) with the WUE recommendation improvement criterion (OBJ-2) constitutes the full verification standard: the model must report honest uncertainty and that uncertainty must be tight enough to produce useful recommendations.

The pilot success criterion (RQ7) is a binary threshold: the RQ5 calibration target must be met on the held-out validation dataset. This is not a subjective assessment; it is computed from the validation data by any third party using standard interval-coverage methods.

The Route B covariation test (RQ9) establishes empirically whether the proxy patch's spectral and physiological time series covaries statistically with the target tomato crop's time series over the growing season. A pre-registered covariation threshold is the pass/fail criterion; failure triggers the Route A contingency path, which is documented as a negative scientific result rather than a project failure.

---

**Identified methodological challenges and intended resolutions**

The project's risk register identifies ten risks across four categories — data access, validation, model complexity, and operationalisation — each with a stated mitigation and contingency. The four challenges of highest evaluative relevance to the methodology are addressed here.

**Challenge 1: Route B's patch-covariation assumption may not hold (RISK-05, probability medium, impact high).** This is the primary scientific risk of the chosen methodology. If the co-located seasonal campaign (RQ9) does not establish sufficient statistical covariation between the proxy patch and the target tomato crop, the Route B premise fails for the chosen patch configuration. The intended resolution is twofold: first, the control-stand variant pre-engineers covariation by deliberately planting a covarying species, making covariation measurable by construction rather than dependent on finding a naturally occurring matching patch; second, Route A is defined within the same modelling framework and can serve as the primary diagnostic pathway if covariation cannot be demonstrated. The negative result — Route B covariation fails for tomato in the chosen Hungarian field configuration — is itself a publishable and valuable contribution to the literature on proxy-based field-state estimation, because it establishes a boundary condition for the Route B approach.

**Challenge 2: Reported uncertainty may not be well calibrated (RISK-06, probability medium, impact high).** The project's headline methodological commitment — an honest uncertainty chain — fails if the uncertainty quantification machinery produces intervals that are systematically overconfident (too narrow) or underconfident (too wide). This risk arises from the inherent difficulty of calibrating complex, multi-source probabilistic models in the presence of irreducible observational noise, model misspecification, and limited validation data. The intended resolution is to build uncertainty-calibration metrics (RQ5) centrally into the validation protocol rather than treating calibration as a post-hoc concern. If the calibration test fails on the initial model, post-hoc recalibration methods (conformal prediction, isotonic regression, temperature scaling) are applied and the calibration process is documented honestly. Claims are restricted to the regime in which calibration is demonstrated.

**Challenge 3: Multi-source spatial and temporal harmonisation (RISK-02, probability high, impact medium).** Sentinel-1 (C-band SAR, 10 m), Sentinel-2 (multispectral optical, 10 m), and PlanetScope (sub-5 m, daily revisit) differ substantially in resolution, revisit cadence, wavelength, and noise. Harmonising these into a coherent analysis-ready time-series stack requires explicit resolution handling, temporal compositing, and quality control. Cloud cover limits Sentinel-2 optical availability (RISK-03); dense vegetation reduces Sentinel-1 SAR retrieval accuracy (RISK-03). The intended resolution is to build the geospatial and time-series data platform (milestone MS1, due month 6) around an explicit quality-control pipeline that weights each sensor contribution according to its per-condition reliability. In cloud-dominated periods, Sentinel-1 SAR is the primary structural signal; in clear-sky periods, the optical streams carry the spectral information. If any one source fails to harmonise reliably, it is restricted to its native resolution or used as a covariate rather than a primary fusion input, and the adjustment is documented.

**Challenge 4: AquaCrop overconfident parameter collapse (RISK-08, probability medium, impact high).** Standard AquaCrop calibration converges on a single parameter set, which collapses the model's parametric uncertainty and propagates overconfident projections into the decision stage. The intended resolution is the uncertainty-aware calibration protocol that retains a posterior distribution over the model's parameters, consistent with established methods in the literature (doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2022.105556). If a full parameter posterior proves computationally intractable within the fellowship's infrastructure, the contingency is to ensemble over a finite set of plausible parameter configurations sampled from the joint posterior, propagate the ensemble spread into the simulation outputs, and report the resulting outcome distributions honestly. The risk is not that the model produces no uncertainty, but that the approximation of the posterior is coarser than intended; this is manageable and documented.

Additional risks — sparse ground truth (RISK-04), cloud and vegetation seasonality (RISK-03), Route A model complexity (RISK-07), sensor calibration integration (RISK-09), and demonstrator pilot scope (RISK-10) — are carried in the project's risk register and mitigated through the design choices already described: field sites secured through AgroVIR before the fellowship begins (RISK-04); sensor weighting per condition (RISK-03); Route B as a credible primary route with Route A as comparison (RISK-07); QC pipeline and sensor comparison in the validation layer (RISK-09); and explicit TRL 3–4 target setting (RISK-10).

---

**Integration of methods and disciplines to pursue the objectives**

The project is genuinely interdisciplinary along two axes, both of which are load-bearing for the research objectives rather than supplementary.

The first axis of interdisciplinarity runs between plant physiology and geoinformatics/remote sensing. These are genuinely distinct scientific disciplines with different methods, instruments, terminology, and publication cultures. Plant physiology grounds the project's validation protocol: the ability to measure chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance using non-destructive instruments on living plants is a domain skill that is not derivable from remote-sensing or data-science competence. Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's doctoral specialisation in the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527) is precisely this domain skill. Without it, the project's validation protocol would be reduced to either destructive biomass or soil-core sampling (which prevents repeated measurement at the same plants) or proxy indicators (which would introduce the unverified assumption the project is designed to avoid). The plant-physiology contribution is not a support function; it is the mechanism by which OBJ-3's verification criteria are made credible.

Geoinformatics and remote sensing grounds the project's diagnostic branch. The ability to process and harmonise multi-resolution SAR, optical, and hyperspectral data streams; to implement probabilistic inference on geospatial data at field scale; to build and maintain a geospatial and time-series data platform; and to interpret satellite-derived signatures in relation to ground-cover type and phenological stage are competences that are not derivable from plant-physiology or crop-science training. Dr. András Jung, Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, brings remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy, and multisensor-drone fusion methods and infrastructure. The Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group he leads (project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29) provides the institutional research environment within which WP1's multi-sensor data integration work is conducted.

The two disciplinary contributions are structurally coupled, not merely co-located. The diagnostic model (Route A or Route B) produces a posterior over the field state; the validity of that posterior is assessed by the plant-physiology ground-truth measurements collected in WP3. The design of the ground-truth protocol (which measurements, at which phenological stages, with which instruments) must reflect an understanding of which physiological signals covary most strongly with the EO observables the diagnostic model uses. This design decision requires simultaneous expertise in both domains: it cannot be executed well by either discipline operating independently. The two-way transfer of knowledge between the fellow and the host group — Dr. Cholakova contributing plant-physiology and stress-phenotyping expertise into the geoinformatics group, and the group contributing EO processing and probabilistic geospatial methods into the fellow's skill set — is therefore not merely a training benefit mandated by the MSCA-PF instrument. It is a methodological precondition for the validation protocol to be scientifically credible.

The second axis of interdisciplinarity runs between crop science and probabilistic machine learning. The FAO AquaCrop model is a domain-specific crop-science model that simulates soil-water dynamics, canopy development, biomass accumulation, and yield under user-specified irrigation schedules and weather inputs. Its parameters — canopy cover curve shape, water productivity, harvest index, root deepening rate — are agronomic quantities with physical meaning. The uncertainty-aware calibration of AquaCrop requires fitting a posterior distribution over these agronomic parameters, which is a probabilistic inference problem (Bayesian or ensemble-based) that draws on probabilistic machine-learning methods not typically encountered in standard agronomic practice. The integration of AquaCrop's domain-grounded simulation structure with probabilistic calibration methods — retaining the model's crop-science interpretability while making its uncertainty explicit — is the specific methodological contribution of WP2 that no single-discipline approach could produce. The literature precedent (doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2022.105556) establishes that such integration is feasible; the project's contribution is the coupling of the calibrated, uncertainty-retaining AquaCrop instance to an upstream probabilistic EO diagnostic and a downstream WUE-optimised decision engine, with the uncertainty chain kept intact across all three components.

The evaluation of whether an interdisciplinary approach is necessary is unambiguous: without plant-physiology expertise, OBJ-3's validation protocol is not credible at the standard this project commits to; without remote-sensing and probabilistic geospatial methods, OBJ-1 cannot be implemented; without crop-science knowledge of AquaCrop's parameters and physical interpretation, OBJ-2 cannot be executed with domain-grounded confidence. All three disciplines are indispensable.

This interdisciplinary design is reflected in the work-package structure. WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state) draws primarily on remote sensing and probabilistic machine learning. WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) draws on crop science (AquaCrop calibration and simulation) and probabilistic methods. WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) draws primarily on plant physiology for the ground-truth protocol and on statistics for the calibration assessment. WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), led by Dr. András Jung with the fellow as participant, is the structural mechanism by which the interdisciplinary exchange is formalised and sustained throughout the fellowship.

---

**Consideration of the gender dimension and other diversity aspects**

The field requirement asks specifically about the gender dimension and diversity aspects as they relate to the content of the research and innovation activities — not team composition.

The core technical content of the diagnostic branch — multi-sensor EO fusion, probabilistic machine-learning inference, geospatial data processing — is not intrinsically gendered: the signal-processing and statistical methods apply identically irrespective of any human characteristic, and the experimental subjects (tomato plants and their physiological indicators) have no gender dimension. Similarly, the AquaCrop model and its uncertainty-aware calibration do not encode gender-specific assumptions.

The application domain — irrigation decision support for smallholder tomato production — does, however, connect to a context in which gender-differentiated impacts are documented in the broader agricultural literature. In many smallholder farming systems, women perform a disproportionate share of field labour and have differential access to irrigation infrastructure, agricultural extension services, and decision-making authority over resource allocation. An irrigation decision-support tool that reduces the information barrier to water-efficient irrigation choices can have gender-differentiated uptake and benefit depending on how it reaches end users, whether it is accessible in terms of technical interface complexity, and whether its outputs are communicated in a form that supports rather than bypasses the decision-making structures within which different groups of farmers operate.

The project addresses this dimension at two levels within its research and innovation content. First, the choice of the research demonstrator format — a standalone web MVP that presents recommendations with their uncertainty in a user-legible form — reflects an explicit design decision to communicate probabilistic outputs accessibly rather than to produce a technically opaque backend system. The accessible output format is a methodological choice that bears on equity of use, because a system that presents only a binary 'irrigate or not' recommendation without uncertainty removes the user's capacity to weigh the recommendation against their own risk tolerance and resource constraints. Presenting the uncertainty enables diverse users — including those with limited access to agronomic advisory services — to exercise informed judgment. Second, the grower-feedback loop through the associated partner AgroVIR provides a mechanism by which the demonstrator's outputs are evaluated from a practitioner perspective that includes Hungarian tomato growers with diverse farm sizes and operational contexts. This feedback is incorporated into the design of the demonstrator's interface and recommendation format as part of WP2 and WP3.

Beyond the application domain, the research methodology is designed to produce open data and open research software released under FAIR principles, which lowers barriers to research access and builds on the project's commitment to diversity of the research community that can subsequently use, critique, and extend the methodology. No research data collection within the project involves human subjects, so the gender dimension does not arise in the context of data collection from or about persons.

In summary: the core EO fusion and probabilistic modelling methodology is not intrinsically gendered, and no justification is required for the absence of a gender dimension in signal processing per se. The application domain — irrigation decision support for tomato farming — connects to a context where gender-differentiated access and benefit are known to arise, and the project's design choices (accessible output format, open outputs, grower-feedback loop through AgroVIR) reflect a considered, if not exhaustive, response to this dimension at the research content level. A more detailed equality, diversity and inclusion plan is to be developed within WP4 in collaboration with the host institution, drawing on Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest's institutional equality framework, and will be documented in the Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3).

---

**Open science practices implemented as an integral part of the methodology**

Open science practices are woven into the project's methodology at three levels: data management, research software, and publication. They are not a compliance addendum to the research plan; they are structural components of the methodology's reproducibility commitment, which is itself required by the project's claim to produce a verifiable, calibrated uncertainty chain.

**Data management and the Data Management Plan.** The project will produce a Data Management Plan (DMP) as deliverable D5-01 (due month 6), a mandatory open-science deliverable under the MSCA-PF instrument and the principal output of milestone MS1. The DMP defines: the provenance and licensing terms for each input data stream (Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 open Copernicus data; ERA5 reanalysis from ECMWF; PlanetScope imagery under the Planet platform access agreement; field observations at Hungarian tomato sites via AgroVIR); the formats and documentation standards for the processed harmonised dataset produced in WP1; the storage, access, and curation arrangements for the field-collected ground-truth dataset (RQ4 measurements: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance) to be produced in WP3; and the embargo arrangements, if any, for any data that cannot be released immediately due to third-party agreements. The ground-truth dataset and the harmonised EO fusion dataset will be released under FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) at the time of the corresponding publication, enabling any independent group to reproduce the validation protocol (RQ5, RQ7, RQ9) from the documented measurement records and data. The DMP is a living document; it will be reviewed at the mid-term point of the fellowship and updated to reflect any changes in data volumes, formats, or access arrangements.

The DMP is specifically grounded in the project's validation commitment. The project claims that the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) is third-party reproducible: this claim is only true if the ground-truth dataset and the model's prediction intervals are openly available for independent recomputation. Releasing the dataset under FAIR principles is therefore not a supplementary open-science gesture but a necessary condition for the reproducibility claim to be credible. This logical dependency — the validity of the reproducibility claim requires open data — is the most direct way in which open science is integral to the methodology rather than parallel to it.

**Open research software.** The diagnostic model (Route A or Route B implementation), the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration code, the counterfactual simulation and WUE scoring engine, and the web MVP demonstrator will be released as open research software with documentation and reproducibility instructions. The open software release serves two methodological functions. First, it enables independent replication: any research group with access to the EO data streams can apply the documented method to a different crop type, a different growing region, or an updated observation period, providing external validation and extension beyond the constraints of the Hungarian tomato pilot. Second, it lowers the barrier for subsequent applied-development programmes targeting higher TRL levels, which is the natural continuation of a TRL 3–4 research prototype (RQ10): the software artefact provides the starting point for such programmes without requiring them to replicate the foundational probabilistic machinery from scratch.

Software development follows reproducible-research practices throughout: version-controlled repositories, documented dependency environments, automated testing of the data processing pipeline, and a structured code-review process within the host group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest. The computational environment for the probabilistic modelling runtime — the Probabilistic Modelling Runtime that supports both Route A and Route B's inference — is containerised and documented to support re-execution on independent hardware.

**Open-access publication.** Research findings will be disseminated through open-access peer-reviewed publications. The milestone MS6 (due month 24) specifies as its verifiable criterion that at least one open-access publication covering the probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework has been submitted, together with release of open data and models under FAIR principles. Publication in open-access venues is the primary mechanism by which the scientific community receives the validated methodology and can compare it against the state of the art established in the systematic literature review underpinning the objectives. Conference dissemination will be directed at venues that reach both the remote-sensing and the precision-agriculture communities, consistent with the project's interdisciplinary profile.

**Training in open science.** The MSCA-PF instrument requires that training activities empower fellows to pursue research careers and prepare them for information-sharing via digital technologies, including open access, FAIR data, and citizen science (scope requirement SR-06). Within WP4 (Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge), the fellow will receive structured training in open-science and FAIR data stewardship as one of the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions (scope requirement SR-05). This training is grounded in the project's own open-science commitments — the fellow implements the DMP, manages the data release workflow, and maintains the open-source repositories — making the training directly applied rather than generic. The responsible use of generative AI tools in remote-sensing analysis, crop-water modelling, and scientific coding is included in the digital-skills training component, ensuring that the fellow's practice with emerging computational methods is grounded in research-integrity principles appropriate to the scientific environment in which they are applied.

**Dissemination and management infrastructure.** WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management) provides the organisational infrastructure for all open-science outputs: managing the DMP lifecycle, coordinating the data and software releases, preparing open-access manuscripts, and communicating results to the relevant audiences — the host's geoinformatics and remote-sensing research community, and Hungarian tomato growers reached through the associated partner AgroVIR. The deliverable D5-02: Dissemination and communication activity report (due month 24) provides the end-of-fellowship record of all dissemination actions executed. Management and coordination are kept lightweight — appropriate for a single-researcher, single-beneficiary MSCA-PF action — with no dedicated management work package budget beyond the two person-months assigned to WP5 in the work-plan seed.

In combination, these open science practices — the DMP by month 6, the FAIR-principle dataset and software releases, the open-access publication commitment, and the fellow's active stewardship of the open-science workflow within the fellowship — ensure that the project's methodological outputs are reproducible, accessible, and appropriately attributed. They constitute the open-science layer of a methodology whose reproducibility is not aspirational but structurally required by its own verification commitments.
