**1.3 Quality of the supervision, training and of the two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host**

---

**The supervision arrangement and its structural logic**

Dr. Rositsa Cholakova is hosted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, under the supervision of Dr. András Jung for a 24-month European Postdoctoral Fellowship. The supervision arrangement is not incidental to the research; it is structurally load-bearing. The project's scientific architecture requires that a researcher with deep experimental expertise in plant physiology and non-destructive stress phenotyping be embedded in a group with operational competence in remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, and multisensor-drone data fusion. Dr. Jung's group supplies precisely the complementary disciplinary infrastructure that the fellow's training history does not cover and cannot be self-acquired within the fellowship period. Conversely, the validation protocol that gives the project's key scientific claim its credibility — the demonstration that the reported uncertainty chain is calibrated rather than nominal — depends on non-destructive physiological measurement expertise that Dr. Jung's group does not hold independently. The supervision arrangement therefore constitutes a genuine interdisciplinary pairing rather than a hosting of convenience: each party brings what the other lacks, and the project requires both.

The supervision is formalised and sustained through WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge, the dedicated MSCA-PF structural work package that runs for the full 24-month duration (months 1–24) under Dr. Jung's lead. WP4 is the organisational backbone through which the Career Development Plan is prepared, the transferable-skills training programme is delivered, and the two-way exchange of methods and knowledge is structured and evidenced.

---

**Supervisor qualifications and track record**

Dr. András Jung holds the position of Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics at ELTE's Faculty of Informatics, Budapest, Hungary. His research expertise spans three tightly coupled domains — remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, and multisensor-drone fusion — all of which are directly relevant to the present project's EO-intensive diagnostic methodology.

Within ELTE, Dr. Jung heads the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group, operating under the national research project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29. This group constitutes the research environment in which WP1's multi-sensor data integration work — the harmonisation of Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, and secured PlanetScope imagery into a geospatial and time-series data platform capable of supporting probabilistic field-state inference — is conducted. The group's infrastructure, methods, and collaborative research culture are the operational substrate through which the host-to-fellow transfer of geoinformatics and remote-sensing competences is delivered in practice, not merely in aspiration.

Dr. Jung's scientific profile extends beyond ELTE into the commercial and entrepreneurial domain: he is co-founder of Cubert GmbH, a company specialising in hyperspectral camera systems, and of Brightic Research. This applied track record is directly relevant to the MSCA-PF instrument's training requirement for knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship (scope requirement SR-05), because it situates the supervisor as someone who has navigated the pathway from fundamental instrumentation research to applied product development — a trajectory that the fellowship's research demonstrator (OBJ-4) must conceptually anticipate even at its TRL 3–4 stage.

Dr. Jung holds habilitations in both Computer Science and Crop Sciences. This dual habilitation is an unusual credential that is institutionally significant for the present project: it establishes formal academic competence in the two disciplines whose junction this project inhabits. The Computer Science habilitation grounds the supervisor's authority over the project's probabilistic machine-learning and data-processing methodology; the Crop Sciences habilitation grounds his ability to supervise the agronomic interpretation of AquaCrop model outputs and the agronomic framing of the irrigation decision engine. A supervisor with both habilitations is therefore able to read the project's outputs across both of its disciplinary axes — remote sensing and crop science — without the fellow needing to broker between two supervisors who do not share a common conceptual frame.

The supervisor's capacity to supervise at advanced level is anchored in his institutional seniority as Deputy Head of the Institute, his leadership of the national Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29), and his commercial co-foundership experience. These indicators collectively demonstrate that Dr. Jung operates as an independent research leader capable of providing the strategic-level guidance that an MSCA-PF European Fellowship requires: not only technical mentoring in EO data processing, but guidance on scientific positioning, publication strategy, and career development appropriate to a researcher targeting post-fellowship independence.

---

**Career Development Plan and the structure of supervision**

The primary instrument of supervision is the Career Development Plan, which is prepared jointly by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and submitted as deliverable D4-01: Career Development Plan at the start of the action (due month 3). The mandatory joint preparation requirement, established by scope requirement SR-07, ensures that the plan reflects the real supervision context — the specific competences and career ambitions of the fellow, the specific research environment and opportunities of the host, and the specific research content of the project — rather than a generic template applied from outside. The Career Development Plan is subsequently reviewed and updated during the fellowship to track progress and adapt the training and career targets as the project's research outcomes become clearer.

The task T4-01 in WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge covers the preparation and review of the Career Development Plan jointly with the fellow (months 1–3, responsible partner: Dr. András Jung). The Career Development Plan encompasses, per SR-07, the fellow's research objectives, training and career needs, transferable-skills development, teaching activities, publication strategy, and open science participation. Because specific quantitative targets for publications, training hours, thesis co-supervision, and similar metrics are to be fixed jointly in the Career Development Plan with the supervisor — consistent with the project's commitment to set targets in the real supervision context rather than pre-determine them without knowledge of the host environment — the Career Development Plan deliverable (D4-01, due month 3) is the correct instrument through which those targets are established. The deliberate deferral of those specific quantitative targets to D4-01 is not a gap in supervision quality; it is a design decision that privileges grounded, jointly-agreed target-setting over generic quantitative aspiration.

The supervisory relationship operates through regular research reviews within the host group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest. These reviews assess the fellow's progress against the scientific objectives of WP1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state, WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration, and WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration, and ensure that the research trajectory remains aligned with the milestones and deliverables established in the project plan. The milestones structure of the project — MS1: Multi-sensor data pipeline operational; Data Management Plan delivered (month 6), MS2: Diagnostic method v1 producing calibrated field-state posteriors (month 12), MS3: Uncertainty-aware decision engine integrated (month 15), MS4: Standalone research demonstrator exercises the end-to-end pipeline (month 18), MS5: Field validation and uncertainty calibration complete (month 22), and MS6: Results disseminated and fellowship outcomes consolidated (month 24) — provides the research-progress backbone against which the supervisory reviews are structured. Each milestone carries a stated verifiable criterion, enabling the supervisor and fellow to assess progress objectively rather than impressionistically.

---

**Planned training activities: scientific, management, and transferable skills**

The training programme is organised through WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge, delivered by Dr. András Jung through task T4-02: Deliver structured transferable-skills training programme (months 1–24, responsible partner: Dr. András Jung). The programme integrates scientific training delivered through active research participation with structured coverage of the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions.

**Scientific training through embedded research participation.** The primary vehicle for Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's scientific training is her active lead role across WP1, WP2, WP3, WP4, and WP5 — effectively the entire project. Within WP1: Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state (months 1–14), the fellow acquires operational competence in geospatial and time-series data platform construction (task T1-01: Acquire and harmonise multi-sensor EO and meteorological data, months 1–6), in the implementation of Route B's homogeneous-patch proxy architecture within a probabilistic modelling framework (task T1-02: Implement Route B homogeneous-patch proxy architecture, months 4–12), and in the calibration of a Bayesian hierarchical model for latent field-state estimation (task T1-03: Calibrate Bayesian hierarchical model for latent field state estimation, months 6–14). These activities transfer to the fellow the host group's methods for multi-resolution EO data harmonisation — specifically the fusion of Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter, Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, and high-resolution PlanetScope data — alongside the probabilistic machine-learning and Gaussian-process inference frameworks through which the project estimates root-zone soil moisture and crop water status as posterior distributions rather than point estimates. These are precisely the competences that Dr. Jung's Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29) holds and that the fellow does not enter the fellowship possessing.

Within WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration (months 6–20), the fellow acquires the crop-modelling and decision-under-uncertainty competences of the project's prognostic branch: uncertainty-aware calibration of the FAO AquaCrop model retaining a parameter posterior rather than a single best-fit set (task T2-01: Calibrate uncertainty-aware AquaCrop model with parameter posterior, months 6–14), counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles (task T2-02: Implement counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles, months 12–17), and the development and integration of the research demonstrator web MVP (task T2-03: Develop and integrate research demonstrator web MVP, months 15–18). The AquaCrop calibration work builds the fellow's competence in uncertainty-aware crop-model analysis, a domain at the interface of crop science and probabilistic inference that neither her doctoral plant-physiology training nor the host's geoinformatics expertise covers in isolation — it is an emergent competence produced by the interdisciplinary pairing.

Within WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration (months 8–24), the fellow contributes her pre-existing non-destructive physiological measurement expertise as the project's scientific input, while simultaneously acquiring the statistical and calibration-assessment methodology needed to evaluate whether the diagnostic model's reported uncertainty is genuinely honest — the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5). Task T3-01 (Design and run field validation protocol on tomato farms, months 8–14), task T3-02 (Collect non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurements, months 10–20), and task T3-03 (Assess uncertainty calibration and patch-covariation assumption, months 20–22) together constitute a complete applied research-methods training sequence in which the fellow designs a validation protocol, executes it across field seasons, and applies it to the evaluation of a probabilistic model — a research competence set that spans the scientific disciplines the project bridges.

Within WP5: Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management (months 1–24), the fellow leads the preparation of the Data Management Plan (task T5-01: Prepare data management plan and open-data/model releases, months 1–6) and the communication and dissemination materials directed at both the remote-sensing/geoinformatics research community and Hungarian tomato growers reached through AgroVIR (task T5-02: Develop communication and dissemination materials for target audiences, months 18–24). Managing the full lifecycle of a Data Management Plan — from provenance documentation for each input data stream through formatting and release standards for processed outputs through open-data deposition under FAIR principles — is a management competence required by the fellowship's open-science commitment and developed directly in the research work.

**Structured coverage of the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions.** Scope requirement SR-05 mandates that training activities integrate key transferable skills common to all fields, including digital skills, generative AI, open science culture, knowledge valorisation, innovation and entrepreneurship, and good scientific conduct. Scope requirement SR-06 mandates that training activities empower fellows to pursue research careers and prepare them for research collaboration and information-sharing via digital technologies. WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge, through task T4-02, operationalises these requirements across five explicit dimensions.

*Digital and AI skills, including the responsible use of generative AI.* The project's core technical competences — probabilistic machine-learning inference on multi-resolution geospatial data, Bayesian hierarchical model calibration, counterfactual simulation over ensemble weather scenarios — are high-dimensional computational tasks that require deep digital competence: proficiency in geospatial data science tooling, probabilistic programming frameworks, remote-sensing data processing pipelines, and numerical simulation environments. These are acquired through hands-on lead responsibility across WP1 and WP2. The responsible use of generative AI tools in the project's three applied domains — remote-sensing analysis, crop-water modelling, and scientific coding — is explicitly included in the digital-skills training component of WP4. This inclusion ensures that the fellow's practice with emerging AI tools is grounded in the research-integrity principles appropriate to scientific environments in which reproducibility, traceability, and honest uncertainty communication are first-order values.

*Knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship.* The research demonstrator (OBJ-4) — the web MVP that integrates the diagnostic and decision pipeline into an accessible user-facing artefact — is the project's primary knowledge valorisation vehicle within the fellowship. Dr. Jung's co-foundership of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research provides direct supervisory mentorship in the pathway from research prototype to applied product, and WP4's training programme includes structured instruction in how the project's uncertainty-aware decision-support methodology could be positioned within the agricultural technology innovation landscape. The fellow is equipped, by the end of the fellowship, to articulate the project's scientific outputs in terms that connect to innovation funding instruments and technology-transfer pathways, consistent with the MSCA-PF instrument's career-development expectations for researchers who may pursue non-academic career routes.

*Research integrity.* The project's foundational methodological commitment — that the reported uncertainty chain must be empirically honest, verified by the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) — is itself an expression of research integrity applied to scientific claims. The validation protocol's pre-registration of success criteria before the fellowship begins, the commitment to report negative results (including a failed Route B covariation test) as publishable scientific findings rather than burying them, and the open-data and open-software releases under FAIR principles are all integrity practices embedded in the research design rather than added as compliance gestures. These practices, modelled by the supervisor and practised by the fellow throughout the project, constitute the substantive research-integrity training that a fellowship at this level provides.

*Open science and FAIR data stewardship.* The fellow manages the full open-science lifecycle of the project: preparing D5-01: Data management plan (due month 6) as part of task T5-01, overseeing the provenance and licensing documentation for each input data stream (Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 open Copernicus data; ERA5 reanalysis from ECMWF; PlanetScope imagery under the Planet platform access agreement; field observations at Hungarian tomato sites via AgroVIR), curating and releasing the field-collected ground-truth dataset under FAIR principles, maintaining the open-source research software repositories, and ensuring that the validation data and model artefacts are openly available in sufficient form that the 90% prediction-interval coverage criterion (RQ5) can be independently recomputed by any third party. This direct stewardship responsibility — not a simulated training exercise but a genuine scientific obligation — is the most effective form of FAIR data training available within a research fellowship.

**Management competence development.** Although WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge assigns only two person-months to the structural training work package, management competence is developed across the full project through the fellow's lead-partner role in WP1, WP2, WP3, and WP5. The fellow coordinates field measurement campaigns with the associated partner AgroVIR (WP3), negotiates and manages the PlanetScope data access agreement (WP1), maintains the open-source repositories (WP2, WP5), and prepares all project deliverables (D1-01: Multi-sensor data harmonisation and diagnostic model report, D2-01: Decision engine and research demonstrator report, D3-01: Field validation and uncertainty calibration report, D4-01: Career Development Plan, D5-01: Data management plan, D5-02: Dissemination and communication activity report). The coordination load of a single-researcher, single-beneficiary MSCA-PF action is proportionate to the fellow's career stage and is designed to develop autonomous research-management competence without creating an administrative burden that displaces scientific work.

---

**Two-way transfer of knowledge between the researcher and the host**

The two-way transfer of knowledge between Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is substantive, bidirectional, and structurally necessary to the project's scientific validity. It is not a token training supplement to an otherwise independent research programme. The exchange operates along two distinct knowledge flows, each of which is load-bearing for the project's ability to meet its stated scientific objectives.

**Fellow-to-host transfer: plant physiology and non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise.** Dr. Rositsa Cholakova contributes to the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics a domain expertise that the group does not hold and cannot replicate without a biologically trained collaborator: the ability to collect, interpret, and scientifically validate non-destructive physiological measurements of drought-stressed tomato plants under field conditions. Her doctoral thesis (summa cum laude, 2020), focused on the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527), established precisely this expertise as her primary scientific contribution: the selection of appropriate instruments (fluorometers for chlorophyll fluorescence, porometers for stomatal conductance, infrared thermometry for canopy and leaf temperature, field spectroradiometers for spectral reflectance), the experimental design of repeated-measure campaigns on living plants, the statistical interpretation of physiological time series in relation to soil water availability, and the understanding of which physiological signals respond earliest and most reliably to the water-stress states the project is attempting to detect from orbit.

This expertise enters the host group in two complementary forms. First, it anchors the validation protocol of OBJ-3: the ground-truth measurements (RQ4) that determine whether the project's probabilistic diagnostic model (OBJ-1) is calibrated, and whether Route B's homogeneous-patch proxy covaries sufficiently with the target tomato crop (RQ9), are credible only if they are collected by a researcher who understands the physiological meaning of each measurement type, the conditions under which each instrument produces reliable readings, and the phenological stages at which different stress indicators are most informative. Without this expertise, the validation data would be a collection of numbers whose interpretive value is uncertain; with it, the validation data constitute a grounded biological reference that gives the calibration criterion (RQ5) its scientific weight. Second, the fellow's knowledge of plant-physiology signals that are detectable by remote sensing — particularly the spectral reflectance signatures that hyperspectral and multispectral instruments observe — transfers into the host group's understanding of the biophysical basis of the EO observables they routinely work with. This is a genuine enrichment of the geoinformatics group's scientific depth: a remote-sensing group that understands why chlorophyll fluorescence and stomatal conductance respond to water stress in the ways that satellite spectral indices reflect can design more targeted observation strategies and interpret satellite-derived vegetation indices with greater biological confidence.

**Host-to-fellow transfer: remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, and multisensor-drone fusion.** In the opposite direction, Dr. András Jung and the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group (ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29) transfer to the fellow the methodological and infrastructural competences in geoinformatics and remote sensing that the project's diagnostic branch requires. These include: operational proficiency in acquiring, quality-controlling, and harmonising multi-resolution EO data streams — specifically the integration of Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter, Sentinel-2 multispectral optical imagery, and high-resolution PlanetScope sub-5-metre imagery into a coherent multi-temporal analysis-ready geospatial stack; probabilistic inference methods applicable to geospatial data, including Bayesian hierarchical modelling and Gaussian-process regression over spatial and temporal covariates; hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy methods relevant to the spectral reflectance ground-truth measurements (RQ4) and to the spectral characterisation of the homogeneous proxy patch (Route B, RQ9); and multisensor-drone fusion methods from the working group's active research programme, which are directly relevant to the project's multi-platform data integration architecture in WP1.

These competences are not available to the fellow through her plant-physiology and crop-monitoring training at Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy. Her doctoral work was grounded in field-scale physiological experimentation, not in EO data processing or probabilistic geospatial inference. The transfer from the host group therefore provides the skills required to execute OBJ-1 — the diagnostic branch — which is the part of the project that the fellow could not execute independently on arrival. By the end of the fellowship, the fellow will have acquired operational competence across the full geospatial data-to-inference pipeline: from raw satellite data ingestion through quality control and harmonisation through probabilistic model calibration through uncertainty-calibrated posterior output. This is the primary career-development mechanism of the fellowship, and it is substantive rather than nominal: the fellow's lead-partner role across WP1 ensures that the transfer is effected through active practice on real data at real field sites, not through observation or coursework alone.

**The interdisciplinary crossing that the two-way transfer achieves.** The outcome of the bidirectional exchange is a researcher with a competence profile that very few individuals in the intersection of precision agriculture and probabilistic Earth observation currently hold: deep experimental knowledge of plant-stress physiology under field conditions, combined with operational proficiency in probabilistic multi-sensor EO fusion and geospatial inference. This combination is directly relevant to the growing need for biologically grounded, uncertainty-aware remote-sensing-based agricultural decision support — a need that is recognised in the literature gap the project targets (the single empty cell at Real-Time Decision Support × PlanetScope in the research-gap matrix of the systematic literature review). It is also a profile that cannot be acquired by training within either discipline alone: plant physiologists who never work with satellite imagery cannot design the EO diagnostic branch; remote-sensing scientists who never work with physiological measurement instruments cannot validate the EO-derived stress indicators against ground truth that has biological meaning. The two-way transfer is the mechanism by which this unusual competence combination is built, and the fellowship is the structural opportunity through which it is achieved.

The two-way transfer is formalised and evidenced within WP4: Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge, under Dr. Jung's lead and with Dr. Rositsa Cholakova as participant. The Career Development Plan (D4-01, due month 3) records the agreed methods-exchange commitments and the mechanisms by which the transfer is tracked during the fellowship. The transfer is not treated as a background benefit of proximity to the host group; it is a first-class component of the fellowship's structure, reflected in WP4's dedicated scope and in the measurable objective OBJ-5: Advancement of the fellow's competences and career, which specifies that two-way transfer of knowledge is to be evidenced by substantive methods exchange between the fellow and the host group.

---

**Non-academic sector placement and secondment**

This European Fellowship does not include a secondment or a non-academic sector placement. The entire 24-month fellowship is conducted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics. This is consistent with scope requirement SR-08 (secondments for European Fellowships are optional) and scope requirement SR-09 (non-academic sector placements are optional with a requirement that added value be explicitly justified when included).

The decision not to include a formal secondment or non-academic placement reflects the project's design constraints: the 24-month fellowship period is fully occupied by the research objectives (OBJ-1 through OBJ-4) and the career-development objective (OBJ-5) without the time cost and logistical complexity of a supervised period away from the host institution. The research demonstrator (OBJ-4, WP2: Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) integrates knowledge-valorisation practice — the construction of an end-to-end prototype that presents irrigation recommendations with their uncertainty in user-legible form — within the fellowship's research work plan rather than requiring a separate non-academic placement to develop that competence. Similarly, the supervisor's co-foundership of Cubert GmbH and Brightic Research, and his dual habilitations in Computer Science and Crop Sciences, provide the innovation and entrepreneurship mentorship that a non-academic placement would otherwise supply, without the administrative and mobility overhead of a formal secondment arrangement.

The associated partner AgroVIR provides farmer access, field logistics, and grower feedback throughout the fellowship's growing-season measurement campaigns (WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), and receives the demonstrator's outputs for evaluation from a practitioner perspective. AgroVIR's involvement in the fellowship is therefore substantive — it is the gateway to the Hungarian tomato farm sites at which the validation protocol (OBJ-3) is executed, and it ensures that the research demonstrator's design is informed by grower perspectives. However, AgroVIR's role is that of an associated partner providing field access and feedback, not a secondment host; the fellow does not undertake a supervised placement at AgroVIR, and AgroVIR does not assume supervisory responsibility for any component of the fellow's research or training. This distinction is deliberate and consistent with the confirmed scope of AgroVIR's participation in the project.

sub_sections.title: Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills
sub_sections.content:
**1.4 Quality and appropriateness of the researcher's professional experience, competences and skills**

---

**Career stage and institutional trajectory**

Dr. Rositsa Cholakova is an experienced researcher approximately four years beyond the award of her doctoral degree, currently positioned at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, Plovdiv, Bulgaria, having trained previously at the Agricultural University - Plovdiv. She holds a PhD awarded in 2020 with the distinction summa cum laude, on the non-destructive evaluation of the physiological status of drought-stressed tomato plants (doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527). The research subject of her doctoral thesis — the non-destructive measurement of physiological water-stress status in the tomato crop — maps directly and without qualification onto the crop species this fellowship targets (research decision RQ1: tomato) and the ground-truth measurement protocol the fellowship requires (research decision RQ4: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance). This convergence is not incidental: it is the specific scientific alignment that makes Dr. Cholakova the appropriate researcher to execute this project, and it is the central argument for the appropriateness of her professional experience.

The fellowship is submitted as a European Fellowship (EF), reflecting the confirmed intra-European Union mobility from Plovdiv, Bulgaria to Budapest, Hungary. Both the mobility rule and the doctoral degree eligibility requirement are satisfied. The fellowship's 24-month duration is the confirmed and appropriate term for the research plan and career-development programme described.

---

**The doctoral foundation: precision relevance to the project's scientific core**

The quality of Dr. Cholakova's doctoral training can be assessed against two distinct dimensions: the intrinsic scientific standard of the work, as evidenced by the summa cum laude award, and its specific relevance to the research functions that the fellowship requires her to perform. Both dimensions are strong, and their coincidence in a single researcher is what makes the fellow-host pairing scientifically compelling.

On the intrinsic standard, a summa cum laude doctoral award indicates examiners' judgment that the thesis constitutes an outstanding and independently conducted original research contribution. The thesis addresses a non-trivial experimental problem — obtaining reliable, biologically interpretable measurements of the physiological condition of drought-stressed living plants without destructive sampling — and does so through the four measurement modalities (chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, spectral reflectance) that are standard instruments of plant ecophysiology and stress research. Each of these modalities requires specific, non-trivial expertise to deploy under field conditions: the correct selection of measurement timing relative to the plant's diurnal cycle and the stress event, the recognition of confounding factors such as ambient light variation, vapour pressure deficit, and canopy architecture that affect each instrument's sensitivity, and the interpretation of the resulting signals in relation to the underlying physiological state rather than instrument artefact. These competences are acquired through extended, practice-based research, not through coursework. The doctoral award at the summa cum laude level confirms that Dr. Cholakova's acquisition of these competences reached a level of excellence at the doctoral stage.

On the specific relevance to the fellowship's research functions, the connection is direct and structural. The project's central scientific claim — that its probabilistic diagnostic model produces honest uncertainty — is operationalised through the uncertainty-calibration criterion (RQ5): 90% prediction intervals produced by the model must contain the ground-truth measurement of crop water status approximately 90% of the time. The scientific validity of this test depends entirely on the quality of the ground-truth reference against which the prediction intervals are compared. If the ground-truth measurements carry unquantified error — because the instruments were operated by someone without specialist expertise, because the measurements were collected at inappropriate phenological stages, or because the instrument readings were misinterpreted in relation to the plant's actual stress state — then the 90% coverage criterion cannot be evaluated reliably. A calibration test is only as credible as the reference it is calibrated against.

Dr. Cholakova's doctoral expertise resolves this methodological risk at its root. Her thesis established her as an expert practitioner of non-destructive physiological measurement of drought-stressed tomato plants — the precise experimental system that the project's validation work involves. The ground-truth dataset collected in WP3: Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration will be produced by the same researcher, using the same measurement modalities, applied to the same crop species under the same stress driver — water deficit — that her doctoral work characterised. There is no residual methodological gap between the fellow's demonstrated expertise and the project's ground-truth requirement. This is the sense in which the fit is not a coincidence of overlapping terms but a direct scientific correspondence between prior training and project need.

The non-destructive character of the chosen measurement methods is itself a methodologically significant design decision that reflects the fellow's training. Non-destructive instruments do not damage or disturb the plant, permitting repeated measurement at the same individual plants over the full growing season. This longitudinal measurement structure is essential for the calibration and validation protocol that OBJ-3 requires: the project needs a temporally dense ground-truth time series across multiple phenological stages and multiple water-deficit levels, so that prediction-interval coverage can be evaluated across the full range of conditions within which the model will be used, not only at a single measurement occasion. Destructive sampling — leaf harvest, soil coring, biomass measurement — would constrain the reference dataset to cross-sectional structure, limiting the statistical power of the calibration test and preventing the repeated-measures design that makes the validation protocol robust. The choice of non-destructive methods, grounded in the fellow's doctoral training, thus produces a methodological advantage for the project that a researcher without this specific background could not provide.

---

**Post-doctoral research trajectory and broadened competences**

In the approximately four years since the award of her doctoral degree, Dr. Cholakova has continued research at the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy, consolidating and extending her experimental expertise in two directions that are both relevant to the fellowship.

The first direction extends the non-destructive physiological assessment approach to additional crop species and stress types. Her peer-reviewed work on maize chilling-stress photosynthesis demonstrates that the measurement capabilities she established for drought-stressed tomato — in particular chlorophyll fluorescence, the primary instrument for measuring photosynthetic function under stress — generalise to the characterisation of physiological stress responses in a different crop (maize) under a different abiotic stress driver (thermal/chilling stress rather than water deficit). This extension is methodologically significant for the fellowship's field validation work for two reasons. First, it establishes that Dr. Cholakova's physiological measurement competences are not narrowly tuned to a single experimental system but transfer across species and stress types; a researcher whose expertise is bounded by a single species in a single stress condition may misinterpret signals when conditions deviate from the training context, whereas the ability to read physiological signals in a second system demonstrates adaptive interpretive capacity. Second, the extension to photosynthesis under thermal stress deepens the fellow's mechanistic understanding of how chlorophyll fluorescence signals — which measure photosystem II efficiency and non-photochemical quenching alongside other photosynthetic parameters — respond to different stress inputs; this mechanistic depth is relevant to interpreting fluorescence signals at the Hungarian tomato field sites, where field conditions will include temperature variation alongside water-deficit stress.

The second direction involves research on biostimulants — compounds applied to plants to enhance their tolerance of or recovery from abiotic stress. This research extends the fellow's expertise from the measurement and characterisation of plant stress status toward an understanding of the mechanistic processes by which plant stress responses are modulated by external interventions. This knowledge is relevant to the field validation protocol in a practical respect: at the Hungarian tomato farm sites accessed through AgroVIR, farm management practices — including the application of plant-health products — will vary between plots and between growing seasons, and the ground-truth measurements must be interpreted in relation to the plants' full stress history and any stress-ameliorating management inputs. A researcher who understands how biostimulant application modifies the trajectory of physiological stress indicators is better positioned to collect measurements that accurately represent the plant's intrinsic water-stress status, distinguishing stress-response signals from management-induced modifications. The biostimulant research background thus adds a layer of interpretive robustness to the fellow's ground-truth data collection that a purely instrument-focused background would not provide.

In combination, these post-doctoral research directions demonstrate that Dr. Cholakova's career trajectory since her doctoral award has been one of deliberate scientific consolidation and extension, not stagnation within the doctoral thesis topic. She has produced independent peer-reviewed research across multiple experimental systems and has deepened her mechanistic understanding of the physiological processes she measures. This trajectory is the mark of a researcher who has achieved post-doctoral independence while remaining grounded in a well-defined domain of expertise — the appropriate profile for an MSCA-PF fellow who will be required to take lead responsibility across the project's research work packages.

---

**Appropriateness of the fellow's experience to each research objective and work package**

The distribution of appropriateness across the five project objectives is differentiated and worth mapping precisely, because the pattern of fit and gap is precisely the pattern that the fellowship's two-way knowledge transfer is designed to address.

For OBJ-3 (Field validation and honest uncertainty calibration) and its associated WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), the appropriateness of the fellow's experience is direct, complete, and sovereign. The scientific content of OBJ-3 is the design and execution of a non-destructive physiological measurement campaign on drought-stressed tomato plants at Hungarian field sites, followed by the assessment of whether the probabilistic diagnostic model's prediction intervals are calibrated against those measurements. This is precisely what Dr. Cholakova's doctoral thesis was about, on the same crop, with the same measurement modalities, under the same stress driver. The only additions are the geographic relocation to Hungary and the connection to a probabilistic EO model rather than a standalone physiological study — neither of which alters the core experimental competence required. OBJ-3 is the fellow's scientifically sovereign contribution: the component that only a researcher with her specific training can execute at the methodological standard the project commits to.

For OBJ-1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the latent field state) and its associated WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), the appropriateness of the fellow's current experience is complementary rather than direct. The diagnostic branch draws on Earth-observation data processing, probabilistic machine-learning inference on geospatial data, and Bayesian hierarchical model calibration — competences that are not part of Dr. Cholakova's plant-physiology training. These will be transferred to her by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, Faculty of Informatics, Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, under the supervision of Dr. András Jung, through her lead-partner role in WP1. The 24-month fellowship duration is sufficient for this transfer to produce operational proficiency, as established in the work plan design: the multi-sensor data harmonisation task (T1-01) introduces the EO data platform and processing environment in the first six months, the Route B proxy architecture task (T1-02) builds probabilistic reasoning in the geospatial context through months 4–12, and the Bayesian hierarchical model calibration task (T1-03) develops the core probabilistic modelling competence through months 6–14. The fellow's starting position for this acquisition is not without foundation: her post-doctoral work on spectral reflectance measurement — one of the four ground-truth modalities (RQ4) — provides a bridge between her plant-physiology domain and the hyperspectral and multispectral remote-sensing methods the host group uses. Spectral reflectance measured by a field spectroradiometer in the plant-physiology context and spectral reflectance retrieved from a Sentinel-2 or PlanetScope image in the EO context are physically the same quantity; the fellow's prior experience with the ground-measured form of this observable provides a conceptual anchor for understanding the satellite-derived form and its relationship to the underlying plant physiological state.

For OBJ-2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine for water-use-efficient irrigation choice) and its associated WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), the appropriateness is again complementary in the EO and probabilistic modelling dimensions but supplemented by an element of the fellow's applied agricultural research background. The FAO AquaCrop model is a crop-science simulation tool that models soil-water dynamics, canopy development, biomass accumulation, and yield in response to irrigation schedules and weather inputs. Its parameters — canopy cover curve shape, water productivity, harvest index, root deepening rate — are agronomic quantities grounded in plant-physiological processes. A researcher who has studied the physiological responses of tomato plants to water deficit is better positioned to interpret the parameters of a crop model calibrated against water-deficit scenarios — and to recognise when the model's parameter estimates are agronomically implausible — than a researcher whose background is exclusively data science or remote sensing. The fellow's crop-physiological background therefore provides a biologically grounded interpretive capacity for OBJ-2's uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration work that contributes to the scientific quality of the calibration outcome.

For OBJ-4 (Standalone research demonstrator (web MVP)) and its associated output within WP2, the appropriateness of the fellow's background is relevant at the interface between research output and practical usability. The research demonstrator is positioned as a TRL 3–4 research prototype (RQ10) that presents irrigation recommendations together with their uncertainty in a form legible to potential end users. Dr. Cholakova's background at an agricultural research institute — the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute, Bulgarian Agricultural Academy — that interfaces with farming practice grounds her understanding of what information growers need and how it is used in agricultural decision-making. This practical grounding, while not a technical competence in the engineering sense, informs the design of the demonstrator's output format and the framing of irrigation recommendations in a way that is relevant to the grower-feedback loop provided through AgroVIR. It is an applied competence that contributes to OBJ-4's quality.

For OBJ-5 (Advancement of the fellow's competences and career), the fellow's career stage and existing competence profile define the starting point from which the fellowship's developmental impact is assessed. At approximately four years post-PhD, with a summa cum laude doctoral thesis, post-doctoral publications extending her plant-physiology expertise to a second crop and a mechanistic domain (biostimulants), and an institutional position at a national agricultural research institute in Bulgaria, Dr. Cholakova is at the career stage at which an MSCA-PF European Fellowship provides maximum developmental impact. She is sufficiently experienced to take independent lead responsibility across the research work packages (WP1 through WP5) and to contribute original scientific judgment to the experimental design and data interpretation, rather than requiring close technical direction at every step. She is simultaneously at a career stage at which the acquisition of a genuinely new disciplinary capability — probabilistic EO data fusion and geospatial inference — through supervised fellowship experience at a leading European geoinformatics group can substantially extend her scientific reach in ways that ordinary career progression within the Maritsa Vegetable Crops Research Institute would not enable within a comparable timeframe. The fellowship, executed at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, under Dr. András Jung's supervision in the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, is precisely the mechanism for this extension.

---

**The productive asymmetry: why the experience gap is a fellowship asset**

The fact that Dr. Cholakova does not arrive at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest already possessing the EO data processing and probabilistic geospatial inference competences of the host group is not a weakness of the proposal — it is the structural rationale for the MSCA-PF fellowship as a career development instrument. An MSCA-PF fellowship that pairs a researcher with a host whose expertise is entirely redundant with her own does not create the two-way knowledge transfer that justifies the instrument; it duplicates a competence that already exists. The asymmetry between Dr. Cholakova's plant-physiology expertise and the host group's EO and geoinformatics expertise is the productive asymmetry from which both directions of genuine knowledge transfer flow: the fellow brings what the host lacks, and the host provides what the fellow lacks, and the project requires both.

This productive asymmetry is what makes the project's scientific architecture — a multi-sensor EO diagnostic model (requiring the host's expertise) validated by non-destructive physiological ground truth (requiring the fellow's expertise) — a genuinely interdisciplinary achievement rather than a single-discipline study with an added measurement component. The appropriateness of the researcher's experience must therefore be assessed not only against the competences she brings but against the competences she will acquire and the scientific value of the combination. The confirmed professional experience described above — doctoral mastery of non-destructive physiological assessment of drought-stressed tomato, post-doctoral extension to a second crop and stress type, mechanistic understanding through biostimulant research, and applied agricultural research practice at a national institute — constitutes the specific experiential foundation on which the fellowship's bilateral knowledge exchange can be built. It is the right experience at the right career stage for this specific fellowship pairing, and it is the experience that makes the project's validation protocol scientifically credible.
